name: Network Security
description: Security of network protocols and infrastructure: routing, DNS, BGP, middleboxes, DDoS, and traffic analysis.

ndss.narrative:
Network security at NDSS has been shaped by two long-running tensions: the growth of encrypted traffic that blinds traditional inspection, and the use of machine learning both to attack and to defend. Kitsune (NDSS 2018) introduced an ensemble-autoencoder approach to online network intrusion detection that could operate at line rate, earning nearly 1,000 citations and setting the benchmark for ML-based detectors.

The 2019–2021 period brought traffic fingerprinting and flow classification into focus. FlowPrint (NDSS 2020) showed that encrypted mobile traffic retains enough structure for app identification; FlowLens (NDSS 2021) made ML-based flow classification efficient enough for production routers; and BGP routing security and lateral-movement detection via temporal graphs rounded out a picture of networks under sustained adversarial pressure.

Recent work reflects the dual-use nature of deep learning in networking. Detecting Unknown Encrypted Malicious Traffic in Real Time via Flow Interaction Graphs (NDSS 2023) showed that graph-based ML can identify novel threats in TLS flows; Large Language Model guided Protocol Fuzzing (NDSS 2024) demonstrated that LLMs can understand protocol semantics well enough to guide network fuzz testing; and papers on IMSI-catcher detection (NDSS 2025) and 5G attack detection (5G-Spector, NDSS 2024) show that cellular network security remains a critical frontier requiring continuous measurement and new analytic tools.

sp.narrative:
Network security at IEEE S&P covers protocol attacks, censorship, routing security, and internet measurement. The 2018-2019 baseline addressed both foundational protocol flaws and large-scale measurement. Tracking Certificate Misissuance in the Wild (S&P 2018) used Certificate Transparency logs to detect unauthorized TLS certificate issuance at internet scale. Breaking LTE on Layer Two (S&P 2019) and Touching the Untouchables: Dynamic Security Analysis of the LTE Control Plane (S&P 2019) jointly revealed that LTE's data and control planes could be attacked without a cryptographic break.

The 2020 cohort demonstrated deep measurement and DDoS defense. ICLab: A Global, Longitudinal Internet Censorship Measurement Platform (S&P 2020) deployed vantage points globally to measure censorship across regimes over years, setting a new standard for longitudinal network measurement. High Precision Open-World Website Fingerprinting (S&P 2020) pushed traffic classification to handle the open-world setting where the monitored page may not be in the attacker's training set.

From 2021, post-quantum readiness and Tor security dominated. Post-quantum WireGuard (S&P 2021) demonstrated a backward-compatible post-quantum VPN. Robust Multi-tab Website Fingerprinting Attacks in the Wild (S&P 2023) and SoK: A Critical Evaluation of Efficient Website Fingerprinting Defenses (S&P 2023) revisited fingerprinting in more realistic multi-tab settings and assessed whether published defenses actually hold.

Throughout the period, S&P network-security papers were distinguished by large-scale empirical rigor: internet-wide scans, longitudinal vantage-point data, and real-operator collaboration rather than lab-only evaluation.

uss.narrative:
The earliest papers in this list (all USENIX Security 2018) show network security split across several long-standing fronts. One thread targets the abuse of core Internet naming and trust infrastructure: FANCI: Feature-based Automated NXDomain Classification and Intelligence (2018) mined non-existent-domain responses to flag DGA malware, while Bamboozling Certificate Authorities with BGP (2018) showed that BGP route hijacks could subvert the web PKI by fooling domain-validation checks. A second thread is measurement and circumvention: End-to-End Measurements of Email Spoofing Attacks (2018) audited how poorly providers authenticate senders, and Quack: Scalable Remote Measurement of Application-Layer Censorship (2018) extended remote censorship measurement beyond DNS/IP blocking. A third thread is anonymity and traffic confidentiality, with NetHide: Secure and Practical Network Topology Obfuscation (2018) hiding topology from traceroute and several Tor-focused papers on performance and covert channels.

Around 2019-2020 the work shifted toward the network's own control and data planes as attack surface. The CrossPath Attack (USENIX 2019) weaponized shared links to disrupt the SDN control channel, and EPIC (USENIX 2020) pushed path-aware architectures where every packet is verified in the data plane. Protocol-implementation security also matured from ad hoc testing into systematic state exploration, exemplified by Analysis of DTLS Implementations Using Protocol State Fuzzing (USENIX 2020), with Composition Kills (USENIX 2020) showing that combining correctly-specified email components still breaks sender authentication.

The early 2020s brought two big breakthroughs. First, programmable switches turned line-rate hardware into a defense platform: Jaqen (USENIX 2021) delivered switch-native volumetric DDoS detection and mitigation, Ripple (USENIX 2021) built a decentralized link-flooding defense, and An Efficient Design of Intelligent Network Data Plane (USENIX 2023) put ML models directly in the data plane. Meanwhile attackers found new amplification vectors, most strikingly in Weaponizing Middleboxes for TCP Reflected Amplification (USENIX 2021), which broke the assumption that reflection attacks needed UDP. Protocol fuzzing also generalized, from Stateful Greybox Fuzzing (USENIX 2022) to packet-sequence-oriented Bleem (USENIX 2023).

The most active recent frontier is the arms race over encrypted-traffic analysis and its defenses, increasingly driven by deep learning. Website fingerprinting moved into realistic settings with Online Website Fingerprinting (USENIX 2022) and was sharpened by robust traffic representations in Subverting Website Fingerprinting Defenses with Robust Traffic Representation (USENIX 2023), while Defeating DNN-Based Traffic Analysis Systems in Real-Time With Blind Adversarial Perturbations (USENIX 2021) and Rosetta (USENIX 2023) attacked and hardened DL classifiers from opposite sides. Censorship research likewise turned to the protocols themselves, as How the Great Firewall of China Detects and Blocks Fully Encrypted Traffic (USENIX 2023) reverse-engineered nation-state filtering of fully encrypted flows. Network security today thus sits at the intersection of programmable infrastructure, ML-based analysis, and the adversarial robustness of both.

top4.narrative:
The earliest papers in this set, all from 2018, mark a turning point where machine learning became the dominant lens for network security. On the defensive side, Kitsune: An Ensemble of Autoencoders for Online Network Intrusion Detection (NDSS 2018) showed that lightweight neural autoencoders could flag intrusions online, while on the offensive side a cluster of traffic-analysis papers used deep learning to break privacy: Deep Fingerprinting (CCS 2018) undermined Tor website-fingerprinting defenses, and DeepCorr (CCS 2018) used neural nets to correlate Tor flows and deanonymize users. Alongside this ML wave, classic infrastructure questions persisted: Anonymity Trilemma (S&P 2018) gave a formal impossibility result bounding anonymity against bandwidth and latency, and FANCI (USENIX 2018) tackled DGA-based malware through NXDOMAIN classification. Several 2018 works also pushed into emerging targets like connected-vehicle traffic control (Exposing Congestion Attack, NDSS 2018).

From 2019 into 2020 the field broadened along two fronts. First, cellular and protocol security matured through formal and layer-level analysis: Breaking LTE on Layer Two (S&P 2019) and 5GReasoner (CCS 2019) systematically attacked mobile-network protocols, while Let's Encrypt (CCS 2019) and work on TLS in censorship circumvention (NDSS 2019) studied the encrypted web at internet scale. Second, censorship measurement became a discipline of its own, with Censored Planet (CCS 2020) and ICLab (S&P 2020) building global, longitudinal observatories. This period also saw infrastructure attacks return to the spotlight: DNS Cache Poisoning Attack Reloaded (CCS 2020) revived a classic attack via side channels, and A Stealthier Partitioning Attack against Bitcoin (S&P 2020) showed AS-level adversaries could split peer-to-peer networks.

A defining shift around 2020-2021 was the move of defenses into programmable hardware. Poseidon (NDSS 2020), Jaqen (USENIX 2021), and Ripple (USENIX 2021) used programmable switches to mitigate volumetric DDoS and link-flooding attacks at line rate, while FlowLens (NDSS 2021) and An Efficient Design of Intelligent Network Data Plane (USENIX 2023) pushed ML classification itself onto the data plane. In parallel, traffic analysis kept escalating as an arms race: TrafficSliver (CCS 2020) split traffic to defeat fingerprinting, Defeating DNN-Based Traffic Analysis Systems (USENIX 2021) used blind adversarial perturbations, and Subverting Website Fingerprinting Defenses (USENIX 2023) restored attacker advantage with robust traffic representations.

Most recently the field has turned reflective and tool-driven. A wave of critical and interpretability work questioned whether ML detectors actually deliver: New Directions in Automated Traffic Analysis (CCS 2021), DeepAID (CCS 2021), and pointedly AI/ML for Network Security: The Emperor has no Clothes (CCS 2022) all interrogated the rigor of learned detectors, while HyperVision (NDSS 2023) advanced unsupervised detection of unknown encrypted threats. At the same time, protocol-implementation testing matured from Stateful Greybox Fuzzing (USENIX 2022) to Large Language Model guided Protocol Fuzzing (NDSS 2024), signaling that LLMs are now being folded into the network-security toolkit. The arc runs from applying deep learning to attack and defend networks, through pushing defenses into programmable infrastructure and measuring the global internet, to a more skeptical, automated, and LLM-assisted present.
